bib.title: You Only Cache Once: Decoder-Decoder Architectures for Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "You Only Cache Once: Decoder-Decoder Architectures for Language Models" (YOCO), Yutao Sun, Li Dong, Yi Zhu, Shaohan Huang, Wenhui Wang, Shuming Ma, Quanlu Zhang, Jianyong Wang, Furu Wei (Microsoft Research, Tsinghua). arXiv:2405.05254v2, 9 May 2024 (arXiv preprint; no venue printed).
COVERAGE: about 54,651 of 54,651 chars read, in 3 passes. Body, appendices A-F and the start of the pseudocode were read. References were only skimmed. Figures 7-10 values come from the extracted axis labels and callouts, not from images.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: The KV cache stores one global layer instead of one per layer, so it is about L times smaller. For a 65B model that is about 80x per token.
  number: ~80x (65B); 24x/32x/40x/64x/80x at 1.2B/6.4B/13B/30B/65B (labels as extracted, in the order of Figure 8's x-axis)
  setup: Figure 8, KV cache KB/token against model size. The Transformer baseline uses GQA. H100-80GB.
  quote: "In particular, the memory of KV caches can be reduced by about 80× for 65B models."
  where: p2 (Intro); Fig 8, p10
- claim: With a 65B model, YOCO can serve 128K tokens in 1GB of GPU memory. A GQA Transformer manages 1.6K tokens in the same 1GB.
  number: 128K vs 1.6K tokens per 1GB
  setup: 65B model size, Transformer with GQA, per the Figure 8 per-token KV cost
  quote: "For example, YOCO can serve 128K tokens with 1GB GPU memory, while Transformer with GQA [ALTdJ+23] can only support 1.6K tokens at 65B model size."
  where: p10
- claim: The intro states the baseline problem: a 65B model's 512K-token KV cache does not fit on one H100.
  number: ~86GB for 512K tokens
  setup: 65B model, GQA, 8-bit KV quantization, H100-80GB
  quote: "For the example of a 65B-size language model (augmented with grouped-query attention [ ALTdJ+23] and 8-bit KV quantization), 512K tokens occupy about 86GB GPU memory, which is even larger than the capacity of one H100-80GB GPU."
  where: p2
- claim: Whole-model inference memory for the 3B model is 9.38x lower at 1M tokens. YOCO uses 12.4GB. At 32K the reduction is about 2x.
  number: 9.38x at 1M; 12.4GB; 1.95x at 32K; 2.32x at 64K; 3.01x at 128K; 4.16x at 256K; 6.39x at 512K
  setup: YOCO-3B (gRet, 26 layers, 24 query heads, 8 KV heads, GQA) against a same-size Transformer with GQA, Flash-Decoding and kernel fusion. H100-80GB. Total memory = weights + activations + KV cache. The last 1,024 tokens are generated.
  quote: "For example of 1M length, the overall inference memory usage is only 12.4GB, while Transformers occupy 9.4× GPU memory."
  where: p10, Fig 7
  (the 4.16x/6.39x/9.38x labels sit on the 256K/512K/1M ticks and 1.95x/2.32x/3.01x on 32K/64K/128K, an inference from the figure layout)
- claim: Prefill latency at 512K context drops from 180s to under 6s. Speedup is 71.82x at 1M, 30.3x at 512K, 15.55x at 256K, 8.36x at 128K, 5.05x at 64K, 2.87x at 32K.
  number: 180s -> <6s at 512K; 71.8x at 1M; 2.87x at 32K
  setup: same as above, 3B model, H100-80GB. The Transformer is optimized (Flash-Decoding, kernel fusion). Gated retention uses chunk size 256 with a Triton kernel. Transformer prefill is about 300s at 1M.
  quote: "Figure 9 shows that YOCO reduces the Transformer prefilling time from 180 seconds to less than 6 seconds for 512K context."
  where: p10-11, Fig 9
  also: "The prefill stage is speeded up by 71.8× for the 1M context and 2.87× for the 32K input." (p2)
- claim: Mechanism for the prefill gain. The cross-decoder only reads the KV cache, so prefill can exit after the self-decoder. That is at least half the layers, and the self-decoder's attention is cheap. Attention prefill goes from O(L·N²·D) to O(L·N·D).
  number: "at least half" of the layers; complexity classes only
  setup: Tables 1-2. The self-decoder is the first L/2 layers.
  quote: "First, only half the layers are needed for forward computation, i.e., at least half prefilling latency reduction."
  where: p5
- claim: Throughput at 512K context is 9.6x higher, 43.1 against 4.5 token/s. The factor is 2.57-2.77x at 32K-128K and 4.37x at 256K (as extracted; the figure label order is ambiguous).
  number: 4.5 vs 43.1 token/s; 9.6x
  setup: counts prefill and generation. The gain comes from faster prefill and from a larger batch, which the freed memory allows.
  quote: "For the example of 512K queries, Transformer's throughput is 4.5 token/s while YOCO reaches 43.1 token/s, i.e, achieving 9.6× speedup."
  where: p11, Fig 10
- claim: Quality is on par with Transformers. Trained at 3B, YOCO-3B averages 0.634 at 1T tokens and 0.636 at 1.6T tokens. OpenLLaMA-3B-v2 gets 0.619 and StableLM-base-alpha-3B-v2 gets 0.612 at 1T tokens.
  number: Eval Harness average 0.634 (1T), 0.636 (1.6T), 0.645 (YOCO-3B-1M)
  setup: 3B model, 2.8B non-embedding params, 26 layers, hidden 3072, trained on 1.6T tokens at 4096 context. Zero-shot, LM Eval Harness. The StableLM-3B-4E1T average is not reported ("—") because its table is incomplete.
  quote: "YOCO-3B 0.379 0.731 0.645 0.689 0.298 0.763 0.639 0.924 0.634"
  where: p7, Table 3
- claim: Validation loss for YOCO scales like a Llama-style Transformer from 160M to 13B. YOCO-gRet beats both the Transformer and YOCO-SWA.
  number: none (curve only; sizes 160M-13B, 10B training tokens)
  setup: 2k sequence length, 0.25M-token batch, 40k steps. SWA window 1,024. Loss figure in Fig 4.
  quote: "YOCO obtains comparable performance from 160M to 13B compared to the Llama-optimized transformer architecture."
  where: p8
- claim: YOCO was extended to 1M context and gets near-perfect single-needle retrieval. In the multi-needle test at 128K, YOCO-3B-1M scores 0.98, 0.98, 0.84 and 0.56 for N=1, 2, 4 and 8.
  number: N=1/2/4/8 = 0.98/0.98/0.84/0.56
  setup: YOCO-3B-1M, 128K test length. Comparison models are LWM-1M-text 7B (1.00/0.90/0.76/0.62), MiniCPM-128K 2.4B (1.00/1.00/0.54/0.56), ChatGLM3-128K 6B (0.94/0.72/0.52/0.44) and YaRN-Mistral-128K 7B (0.02/0.12/0.08/0.20). Extension schedule is 64K/256K/1M with 6B/4B/1.5B tokens. No long-instruction tuning data.
  quote: "YOCO-3B-1M 3B 0.98 0.98 0.84 0.56"
  where: p8, Table 4; Table 7 p18

LIMITS
- The profiled models are 3B, except Figure 8, which gives per-token KV cost across sizes. The 80x claim for 65B is a per-token ratio, not a measured end-to-end run at 65B.
- The paper sets the 1.2B to 65B ratios (24x to 80x) next to L. The authors say the "reduction ratio becomes larger as the number of layers increases".
- The "once" is global KV only. Footnote 2 concedes the self-decoder still holds a constant-size cache: "Strictly, self-decoder also needs to store a certain number of caches."
- The baseline is a Transformer with GQA, Flash-Decoding and kernel fusion. Measurements are on H100-80GB only, with 1,024 generated tokens. There is no comparison against other KV-reduction methods (quantization, eviction, MLA) and no combined results.
- The scaling-curve comparison uses small token budgets (10B tokens). The 3B comparison uses 1T and 1.6T tokens against models from other labs.
- Quality evidence is limited to Eval Harness zero-shot, needle retrieval and NLL curves. There are no long-context downstream benchmarks and no instruction tuning.
- It needs a new architecture trained from scratch, so it cannot be applied to existing checkpoints.
- Future-work items (YOCO + BitNet + Groq, multimodal, cache compression/indexing) are proposals, not results.

BUILDS ON: Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017, [VSP+17]); grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al. 2023); Flash-Decoding (Dao, Haziza, Massa, Sizov 2023); retention/RetNet (Sun, Dong, Huang et al. 2023, [SDH+23]); sliding-window attention (Child et al. 2019); GateLoop (Katsch 2023) for the data-controlled decay; StableLM-3B-4E1T training recipe; Llama (Touvron et al. 2023); Kaplan et al. 2020 scaling laws; Jamba (Lieber et al. 2024) for the hybrid finding; needle-in-a-haystack (Kamradt 2023) following the Gemini 1.5 and LWM settings; Fu et al. 2024 for long-context data up-sampling.

CODE: Appendix F pseudocode (gated retention in parallel, recurrent and chunkwise forms). Appendix F begins on p18 with "def ParallelRetention(q, k, v, gt)", which uses logsigmoid and a causal mask. The core recurrence is Eq. 5, "Sn = γnSn−1 + K⊺nVn; gRet(Xn) = QnSn". Eq. 2-3 show cross-decoder KV sharing: "K̂ = LN(X^{L/2})WK, V̂ = LN(X^{L/2})WV".

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p1): bar charts of GPU memory, throughput and prefill latency at 512K, YOCO against Transformer. Labels are 6.4X, 30.3X and 9.6X (the 6.4X and 30.3X values match the 512K points in Figs 7 and 9; it is a quick summary of the headline results).
- Fig 2 and Fig 3 (p3-4): architecture, and the early-exit prefill flow. The best visual for the idea of "cache once".
- Fig 7 (p10): memory against length, with a 1M breakdown into weights, KV cache and other.
- Fig 8 (p10): KV KB/token against model size, 24x to 80x.
- Fig 9 (p11): prefill time against length, with speedup labels.
- Fig 10 (p11): throughput against length.

PROBLEMS: Tables and figure labels were extracted as scattered numbers, so the Fig 7-10 mappings of ratios to lengths are inferred from axis order. Figure 1's 6.4X is consistent with the 512K point of Fig 7. The text itself says nothing of the 64K to 128K throughput labels. No embedded instructions found.
